source: Moray (1959) Attention in dichotic listening: affective cues and the influence of instructions
finding: Own name in the ignored ear was noticed by only a minority. It is the base rate for later replications.
numbers: About 33% (4 of 12) reported own name in the unattended message, as cited by Conway 2001 and Roer and Cowan 2021.
limits: Tiny sample. Value taken from the replication papers I opened, not the original.
agent_relevance: Strong cues break through but rarely. Do not assume strict filtering or free access to everything.

source: Wood and Cowan (1995) The cocktail party phenomenon revisited
finding: Replicated Moray with better equipment.
numbers: 34.6% reported own name in the irrelevant message (figure quoted by Conway 2001).
limits: Retrospective report only. Cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: Break-through is real but under half of people.

source: Conway, Cowan, Bunting (2001) The cocktail party phenomenon revisited: the importance of working memory capacity
finding: Name detection in the unattended channel depends on working-memory span. Low-span people notice their name more.
numbers: 20% of high-span vs 65% of low-span subjects reported hearing their name. Groups were upper and lower operation-span quartiles. Fisher exact test significant. Name came at 4 or 5 min of shadowing, with a yoked control name.
quote: subjects who detect their name in the irrelevant message have relatively low working-memory capacities
limits: Extreme quartiles only; small groups; self-report afterwards.
agent_relevance: Better capacity means tighter filtering. Leak into context is a failure of inhibition.

source: Conway, Cowan, Bunting (2001), design note
finding: The paper frames the effect as inhibition: low-span people fail to block distractors.
numbers: Abstract and intro state Moray 33% and Wood and Cowan 34.6% as the prior rates. Task was shadowing a relevant message while a name was inserted.
limits: I read the abstract, intro, method and first results only.
agent_relevance: Distractor sensitivity is an individual-difference trait; expect it to vary with model capacity.

source: Roer and Cowan (2021) A preregistered replication and extension of the cocktail party phenomenon: one's name captures attention, unexpected words do not
finding: Preregistered replication confirmed own-name break-through but found no capture by semantically unexpected words.
numbers: N = 80 after 2 exclusions. 23 participants (29%) reported own name. Only 1 noticed an unexpected word and could not report it. Cited comparisons: 33% Moray, 35% Wood and Cowan, 43% Conway (quartile average), 58% and 48% Naveh-Benjamin 2014 (young adults).
quote: One's own name attracted and captured attention of some individuals ... whereas semantically unexpected words did not.
limits: German speakers; Bayesian tests in JASP.
agent_relevance: Only high-priority personal stimuli leak. Generic surprising content does not. Fits attenuation with thresholds, not pure late selection.

source: Roer and Cowan (2021), working-memory moderator
finding: The span effect did not replicate in detection reports but did in shadowing errors.
numbers: Bayes factors for low vs high span name detection: BF10 = 1.023, 0.582, 1.018 (inconclusive). Lowest quartile operation span M = 28.00 (range 10-39) vs 8.22 (6-12) in Conway. Low-span still made more shadowing errors, strongest with both span measures combined.
limits: Range restriction in the low quartile is the authors' explanation. Not a clean failure.
agent_relevance: Moderators need the true low end of capacity. Sub-awareness break-through can occur without report.

source: Roer and Cowan (2021), time course of capture
finding: Attention recruitment by the name was brief.
numbers: Shadowing errors rose at the name position and the next two words. No difference three words later and none on the word just before the name.
limits: Word-level error counts.
agent_relevance: Break-through is a short interruption, so a single re-check may recover from it.

source: Li, Lee, Chiu, Loeb, Sanderson (2024) Attention capture by own name decreases with speech compression
finding: Own name slows a visual word-categorisation task even when heard as a background distractor. Time-compression weakens the effect.
numbers: Exp 1 N = 39: slowing by over 100 ms with own name versus other names or none. Exp 2: N = 25 per compression level, three levels. Slowing strongest with slight compression, weakest with intense. At 38% compression F(2,46)=5.11, p=.01, partial eta squared .182.
limits: Different paradigm (visual task plus audio distractors), so not a direct dichotic test.
agent_relevance: Capture is graded by signal quality. Degraded input gets less priority.

source: Snowden and Gray (2025) Reduction in distraction due to perceptual load: a failure to replicate
finding: Six experiments did not find that high perceptual load removes distractor effects. This was the main test between early and late selection under load theory.
numbers: Six experiments, for example Exp 2 N = 32. Central distractors gave strong distraction and congruence effects at all loads. Peripheral distractors gave weaker effects. Effects were independent of load.
quote: Our findings thus do not support the tenants of perceptual load theory
limits: Authors' own series; display details may matter. Many earlier studies did find the effect (Murphy et al. 2016 cited).
agent_relevance: The middle path (load decides early vs late) is shaky. Hard tasks do not guarantee filtering.

source: Marciano and Yeshurun (2017) Large inter-individual and intra-individual variability in the effect of perceptual load
finding: Reanalysis of 8 experiments at the individual level found few people who followed load theory. Seven observers tested 5 times each changed pattern across sessions.
numbers: 8 experiments reanalysed; 7 observers x 5 identical sessions. Few participants matched the prediction. Often interference was larger at high load, and sometimes a reversed compatibility effect appeared.
quote: all seven participants showed large between-sessions variations
limits: Small repeated-measures sample (7).
agent_relevance: Group averages can hide unstable effects. Test an agent scaffold on many seeds.

source: Chen and Cave (2013) Perceptual load vs. dilution: the roles of attentional focus, stimulus category, and target predictability
finding: Four experiments. Adding neutral items cut distractor processing only in some conditions, so neither load nor dilution alone explains it.
numbers: Set size reduced distractor processing only with broad attentional focus, same-category neutral items and weak preknowledge of the target.
limits: I read the abstract and intro; method details skimmed.
agent_relevance: Rival account: clutter dilutes a distractor rather than using up capacity. In a prompt, extra similar-category text could do either.

source: Tsal and Benoni (2010) dilution account (as described in Snowden and Gray 2025)
finding: Dilution account: distractor effects drop with extra neutral items because they degrade the distractor signal, not because capacity runs out.
numbers: Per Snowden and Gray intro: some low-load versions fail to give any distraction (Eltiti 2005, Johnson 2002, Tsal and Benoni 2010).
limits: Second-hand description; the original was not opened.
agent_relevance: Discriminating test: manipulate item similarity while holding load fixed.

source: Lachter, Forster, Ruthruff (2004) Forty-five years after Broadbent: still no identification without attention
finding: Argued that apparent late-selection evidence comes from attention briefly shifting to the unattended item. Supports early selection with leakage.
numbers: No numbers recorded this session.
limits: Not opened; paywalled. Summary from memory.
agent_relevance: Leaks may be shifted attention, not parallel processing.

source: Treisman (1960) Contextual cues in selective listening
finding: Attenuation theory source. When a sentence switched ears, listeners followed the meaning into the wrong ear.
numbers: Numbers not recorded this session.
limits: From memory; not opened.
agent_relevance: Meaning, not just channel, steers selection. Attenuated input keeps thresholds.

source: Gray and Wedderburn (1960) Grouping strategies with simultaneous stimuli
finding: Split-message study. People recalled by meaning across ears.
numbers: Numbers not recorded this session.
limits: From memory; not opened; later debated as switching rather than parallel processing.
agent_relevance: Selection can follow semantics.

source: Deutsch and Deutsch (1963) Attention: some theoretical considerations
finding: Late selection: all input is identified, then chosen by importance.
numbers: No numbers (theory paper).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A late filter predicts everything in context is processed, so selection happens at response.

source: Corteen and Wood (1972) Autonomic responses to shock-associated words in an unattended channel
finding: Skin response to shock-paired words in the unattended ear, even for related words, was cited as late-selection evidence.
numbers: Numbers not recorded this session.
limits: From memory; Holender (1986) criticised awareness checks.
agent_relevance: Sub-awareness processing may exist.

source: Holender (1986) Semantic activation without conscious identification
finding: Critique: evidence for unattended semantic processing lacked proper awareness checks.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Late-selection claims need strict controls.

source: Cherry (1953) Some experiments on the recognition of speech, with one and with two ears
finding: Founding dichotic shadowing study. Listeners reported physical features of the ignored ear but not its content.
numbers: Numbers not recorded this session.
limits: Cited from the intro of Conway 2001, which I opened. The original was not opened.
agent_relevance: Origin of the filter idea.

source: Broadbent (1958) Perception and Communication
finding: Single-channel early filter selects on physical features before meaning.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Strict form is contradicted by name break-through.
agent_relevance: Keep any filter soft.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (GSM-IC)
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to grade-school math problems cut accuracy, and few problems stayed solved across all distractor types.
numbers: code-davinci-002, chain of thought: micro accuracy 72.4%, normalized 76.2%, macro 6.0%. With instruction: 77.8%, 81.8%, 15.0%. Least-to-most plus instruction: 80.6%, 85.7%, 25.0%. text-davinci-003 base accuracy 80.0 (CoT) and 81.0 (LTM). Fewer than 30% of base problems consistently solved.
quote: fewer than 30% of the base problems are consistently solved after adding distractors
limits: GPT-3 family models from 2022; synthetic distractors (GSM-IC-4K).
agent_relevance: LLMs act like late-selection systems: all context is processed and irrelevant numbers leak.

source: Shi et al. (2023), mitigations
finding: What helped: self-consistency, exemplars that contain distractors, and an instruction to ignore irrelevant text.
numbers: Self-consistency with 20 samples: more than +11 points overall micro accuracy, +35.5 points for 0-COT. Correct answer in 99.7% of 20 samples (96.5% for 0-COT). Best macro accuracy still only 45%.
limits: 2022-era models.
agent_relevance: Sampling plus an explicit relevance instruction are cheap to add to a scaffold.

source: Shi et al. (2023), role-overlap boundary condition
finding: Distractors that share entities with the problem hurt most.
numbers: text-davinci-003 macro accuracy fell to 0 on problems with more than 2 steps when the irrelevant sentences had role overlap.
limits: One model.
agent_relevance: Similar distractors act like same-category flankers in human load studies.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: Two steps: rewrite the context to keep only relevant parts, then answer. This is an explicit early filter.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B-chat. Factuality with a distractor opinion 62.8% to 80.3% (oracle 82.0%). GSM-IC in-topic distractors 51.7% to 61.3%; about +12 points random and +10 in-topic. Instruction to ignore gave no consistent improvement. 200 prompts graded by GPT-4; math averaged over 3 seeds.
limits: Extra inference cost; one open model.
agent_relevance: Filter-then-reason beat ignore-it instructions here. This conflicts with Shi 2023, where instructions helped.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023), ablations
finding: Keeping the original context beside the filtered one removed part of the gain. A single-step variant was weaker.
numbers: Keep-original variant 74.5% vs S2A 80.3%. Single-step variant 71.7% vs baseline 62.8% on factuality.
limits: Numbers from the ablation text; one model.
agent_relevance: Hard removal beats soft ignoring. This echoes early selection.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Accuracy is highest when the relevant item is first or last and drops in the middle, a U shape like serial-position effects.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA can fall by more than 20% in the worst case; at 20 and 30 documents it is below the closed-book 56.1%. Closed-book/oracle: GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.1/88.3, Claude-1.3 48.3/76.1, LongChat-13B 35.0/83.4, MPT-30B 31.5/81.9.
limits: 2023 models. Extended-context variants performed nearly the same as short ones when the input fit.
agent_relevance: Put key facts at the start and end of the prompt and keep context short.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Focus Directions Make Your Language Models Pay More Attention to Relevant Contexts
finding: A small set of attention heads controls how much weight relevant context gets. Raising their attention reduces distraction.
numbers: Top-20 heads with split-softmax exponent 0.3: exact match 59.4% to 67.1%. Random heads: under 0.3% change. Another task: 52.67% to 62.00% after post-training. Distraction caused by an irrelevant high-scoring passage dropped EM from 67.0% to 65.1%.
limits: Needs white-box access and relevance labels. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Mechanistic view of attenuation as gain on relevant context. Not usable through an API, but suggests relevance tags.

source: Koo (2026) Can Large Audio-Language Models Ignore Multilingual Distractors? (MUSI)
finding: Cocktail-party benchmark for audio LLMs. Errors are mostly following the wrong stream, and separating sources first does not fix attribution.
numbers: Open-weight models chose the distractor stream for 21.5-41.0% of items at 0 dB, accuracy near 0.016 with ECE about 0.73. Separation-based accuracy was stable across SNR; cocktail-party accuracy fell sharply at negative SNR. Gemini-2.0-Flash separation 0.952 yet worst cocktail-party accuracy. Korean distractors gave the least interference.
limits: Six models; multiple choice; arXiv preprint.
agent_relevance: Models can confidently follow the wrong source. Add an explicit source-tag step.

source: Koo (2026), target selection and calibration
finding: Interference damages calibration as well as accuracy. Misselection persists even when separation is good.
numbers: Target-selection ratios at 0 dB: 59.0% Qwen2-Audio, 78.5% MERaLiON-2, 78.1% Audio-Flamingo-3, 68.9% Qwen2.5-Omni. ECE for Audio-Flamingo-3 rose from about 0.03 to about 0.14. Misselection persisted at +10 dB where SI-SDR was above 16 dB.
limits: Text extraction was noisy for the ECE figures.
agent_relevance: Confidence cannot be trusted when sources compete.

source: Meng et al. (2024) Large Language Model Can Transcribe Speech in Multi-Talker Scenarios with Versatile Instructions (MT-LLM)
finding: An LLM (Llama 2 backbone, LoRA, WavLM and Whisper encoders) can follow instructions to transcribe a chosen talker in mixed speech.
numbers: About 7.55 billion parameters, 1% (76.6 million) trainable. Six instruction types: multi-talker, target talker, sex, order, language, keyword. About 6.3K hours of speech.
limits: Trained system, not a test of a general LLM. I did not extract the WER table.
agent_relevance: Selection by instruction is learnable. This is top-down attention control.
